concept.name: Type Systems & Generics

relationships.description: Connects Type Systems & Generics to jvm internals and garbage collection in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Generics parameterize types over other types so you write one algorithm or container while preserving static type safety, implemented via type erasure (Java), monomorphization (Rust/C++), or CLR reification (C#).
spark.keyTakeaway: Type erasure keeps binaries small but loses runtime type info and boxes primitives; monomorphization gives zero-cost specialization and inlining at the expense of compile time and binary size.

concept.whyItMatters: Generics eliminate unsafe `Object`/`void*` casts and duplicated boilerplate across collections, async futures, and API wrappers—while their compilation strategy directly determines memory layout, CPU cache density, and compile times.
whenToUse: Reusable containers, parsers, and algorithms (`Vec<T>`, `List<T>`, `Result<T, E>`) whose logic is independent of the element type.
Encoding invariants at compile time via phantom types or bounded type parameters (e.g., `Connection<Authenticated>` vs `Connection<Unauthenticated>`).
Library APIs where callers need type-safe return types inferred from inputs without runtime downcasting.
whenNotToUse: Heterogeneous collections where elements have different concrete types at runtime (use trait objects `Box<dyn Handler>` in Rust or interfaces in Java/Go).
Simple internal helpers used with only one concrete type; premature genericization with 4+ type bounds obscures error messages and slows compilation.
Deeply nested C++ template metaprogramming where `constexpr` functions or straightforward runtime polymorphism would be far more maintainable.
keyPoints: **Type Erasure (Java, TypeScript)**: The compiler checks `<T>` statically and erases it to `Object` (or its upper bound) in bytecode/JS; you cannot do `new T()` or `x instanceof List<String>`, and primitives (`int`) must be boxed (`Integer`, 16+ bytes heap overhead) until Project Valhalla.

**Monomorphization (Rust, C++, Zig)**: The compiler emits a dedicated machine-code copy for each concrete `T` (`Vec<u64>`, `Vec<String>`), enabling unboxed contiguous memory, SIMD, and full inlining—at the cost of larger binaries and slower builds.

**Reified Generics (C# CLR, Kotlin `inline reified`)**: The .NET CLR preserves generic type arguments at runtime, specializing value types (`List<int>`) without boxing while sharing machine code across reference types (`List<string>`, `List<object>`).

**Variance** controls subtyping through generics: Covariance (`out T` / `? extends T`) is safe for producers/readers; Contravariance (`in T` / `? super T`) is safe for consumers/writers (PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super); mutable containers (`List<T>`) must be invariant.
**Bounded Polymorphism** (`T extends Comparable<T>` in Java, `T: Ord` in Rust, `[T comparable]` in Go 1.18+) restricts `T` to types supporting required operations while keeping type safety.

examples.title: Java Heap Boxing vs. Rust Monomorphized Layout
examples.scenario: Storing 10 million 64-bit timestamps in Java `ArrayList<Long>` vs. Rust `Vec<u64>`.
examples.outcome: Java's type erasure forces `Long` heap objects (16-byte object header + 8-byte payload + 4–8 byte reference = ~240–320 MB scattered on the heap with GC pressure); Rust's monomorphized `Vec<u64>` packs 80 MB contiguously in a single allocation with zero pointer chasing.

examples.title: PECS Variance Bug in Java Collections
examples.scenario: A library method `void pushAll(List<Number> dst, List<Integer> src)` fails to compile when passing `List<Integer>` for `dst` or `List<Object>` for `dst`.
examples.outcome: Changing the signature to `void pushAll(List<? super Number> dst, List<? extends Number> src)` makes `src` covariant (producer) and `dst` contravariant (consumer), accepting both `List<Integer>` sources and `List<Object>` destinations safely.

tradeOffs.pro: Monomorphization delivers zero-cost abstraction: unboxed structs, inlineable comparators, and no virtual dispatch.
tradeOffs.con: Code bloat increases instruction-cache (I-cache) pressure and stretches compile/link times compared to single-copy erased bytecode.

tradeOffs.factor: Static Generics vs. Dynamic Dispatch (`dyn Trait` / Interface)
tradeOffs.pro: Generics allow static dispatch and compiler specialization.
tradeOffs.con: Dynamic dispatch supports heterogeneous slices (`Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>>`) and keeps binary size small when 50+ implementations exist.

tradeOffs.factor: Structural vs. Nominal Typing (TypeScript vs. Java/Rust)
tradeOffs.pro: TypeScript structural generics (`<T extends { id: string }>`) compose effortlessly across third-party DTOs without shared interfaces.
tradeOffs.con: Structural compatibility can accidentally accept unrelated shapes that happen to share field names, requiring branded types for strict IDs.

failureModes.name: Heap Pollution via Unchecked Casts & Raw Types
failureModes.description: Mixing raw `List` with `List<String>` in Java compiles with a warning and fails later with a `ClassCastException` far from the bug site.
failureModes.mitigation: Treat `-Xlint:unchecked` as a compiler error, ban raw types in lint rules, and use `Collections.checkedList` at untrusted boundaries.

failureModes.name: Instruction Cache Thrashing from Over-Monomorphization
failureModes.description: A large Rust async state machine or generic parser instantiated across 40 concrete types bloats `.text` by megabytes and causes L1i cache misses.
failureModes.mitigation: Factor non-type-dependent logic into a non-generic inner function (the 'polymorphization' / thin-wrapper pattern, e.g., `fn inner(slice: &[u8])`).

failureModes.name: Covariant Array Unsoundness
failureModes.description: Java/C# treat arrays as covariant (`String[]` is a `Object[]`), allowing `Object[] a = new String[1]; a[0] = 42;` to compile and crash at runtime with `ArrayStoreException`.
failureModes.mitigation: Prefer invariant generic collections (`List<T>`, `Span<T>`) over mutable arrays in public APIs.

failureModes.name: TypeScript Recursive Generic Depth Explosion
failureModes.description: Deeply nested conditional/mapped types (e.g., 10-level ORM query builders) hit `TS2589: Type instantiation is excessively deep` and freeze IDE language servers.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap recursion depth, simplify inference helpers, and benchmark `tsc --generateTrace` on slow modules.

commonMistakes: Confusing `List<Object>` with `List<?>` in Java—`List<String>` is *not* a subtype of `List<Object>` because `List` is invariant.
Trying to inspect `T.class` or instantiate `new T()` inside an erased Java generic method instead of passing a `Class<T>` token.
Adding unnecessary `T: Clone + Send + Sync` bounds on Rust struct definitions rather than only on the `impl` blocks that actually need them.
Using `any` or `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` to silence generic variance errors instead of fixing the producer/consumer wildcard.
In Go, reaching for `[T any]` generics with reflection inside the body instead of a clean interface.

sections.content:
## The idea

Parametric polymorphism (generics) lets functions and data structures abstract over **types** the same way functions abstract over **values**. Instead of writing `IntList` and `StringList`, you write `List<T>` once and let the compiler verify every call site.

The key design divide across languages is **what happens at compile time**:
- **Type Erasure** (Java, TypeScript): Check types at compile time, then erase `T` to a single shared representation (`Object` or JS object) at runtime.
- **Monomorphization** (Rust, C++, Zig): Stamp out specialized code for every concrete `T` used in the program.
- **Hybrid / Reified** (C# CLR, Go 1.18+ GC-shape stenciling): Share code for pointer-shaped types while specializing value types (`int`, structs).

## Concrete walkthrough

Compare compiling `fn max<T: Ord>(a: T, b: T) -> T` in Rust vs. `<T extends Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b)` in Java:

1. **Rust (Monomorphization)**: If your binary calls `max(3u64, 7u64)` and `max("a", "b")`, `rustc` generates two concrete symbols (`max::<u64>` and `max::<&str>`). `max::<u64>` compiles down to a single `cmp` + `cmov` CPU instruction with zero heap allocation or virtual call.
2. **Java (Type Erasure)**: `javac` compiles one bytecode method `Comparable max(Comparable a, Comparable b)` and inserts an implicit `checkcast` at each call site. Calling `max(3, 7)` boxes both `int`s into `Integer` objects on the heap and invokes `Integer.compareTo` via interface dispatch (`invokeinterface`).

sections.content:
## Variance: Covariance, Contravariance, Invariance

Given `Dog <: Animal` (Dog is a subtype of Animal), how does `Box<Dog>` relate to `Box<Animal>`?

- **Covariant (`+T`, `? extends T`, `out T`)**: `Producer<Dog> <: Producer<Animal>`. Safe when `T` only appears in **return (output)** positions. Example: `Iterator<Dog>` can safely be read wherever an `Iterator<Animal>` is expected.
- **Contravariant (`-T`, `? super T`, `in T`)**: `Consumer<Animal> <: Consumer<Dog>`. Safe when `T` only appears in **parameter (input)** positions. Example: a `Comparator<Animal>` can safely compare two `Dog`s.
- **Invariant (`T`)**: Neither is a subtype of the other. Required whenever `T` is both read and written (e.g., `List<T>` or `AtomicReference<T>`), preventing you from inserting a `Cat` into a `List<Dog>`.

## Generic implementation strategies across languages

| Language | Strategy | Runtime Type Info (`T` known?) | Primitive Boxing? | Binary Bloat | Signature Feature |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Java (pre-Valhalla) | Type Erasure | No (erased to bound) | Yes (`int` → `Integer`) | None | Use-site variance (`? extends`, `? super`) |
| C# (.NET CLR) | Reified + JIT Specialization | Yes (`typeof(T)`) | No (specialized per struct) | Low (shared for ref types) | Declaration-site variance (`in`/`out`) |
| Rust | Monomorphization | Only via `TypeId` / `'static` | No (unboxed) | High if unchecked | Trait bounds (`T: Ord + Send`) |
| Go 1.18+ | GC-Shape Stenciling + Dict | Partial (via dictionary) | No for same-shape structs | Moderate | Structural type sets (`~int \| ~int64`) |
| TypeScript | Structural Erasure | None (erased in JS output) | N/A (JS values) | None | Mapped & conditional types |

## Failure modes

Generic abstractions break down in two opposite ways: **compile-time complexity** and **runtime overhead**:

- **Monomorphization bloat**: In large Rust or C++ services, generic HTTP handlers or JSON serializers instantiated for 100 DTO types bloat binaries by tens of megabytes and hurt instruction-cache hit rates.
- **Over-abstracted type gymnastics**: Encoding complex business state machines in nested conditional types (TypeScript) or trait-level Peano arithmetic makes compiler errors unreadable (`expected _, found _`) and slows down team velocity.

## Taming bloat: The thin-wrapper pattern

In Rust and C++, you get both ergonomic generic APIs and fast builds by splitting generic functions into a tiny inlineable wrapper and a non-generic core:

- **Outer generic shell**: `pub fn read_config<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<Config>` simply calls `read_config_impl(path.as_ref())`.
- **Inner monomorphic core**: `fn read_config_impl(path: &Path) -> Result<Config>` is compiled **once** regardless of how many `PathBuf`, `&str`, or `String` types callers pass.

In Java, Valhalla's value classes (`value class`) aim to bridge the opposite gap by letting `List<Point>` store flat unboxed structs without changing generic syntax.

## Practical checklist

- Keep generic bounds minimal on struct definitions; place behavioral bounds (`Ord`, `Serialize`) only on the `impl` blocks or methods that require them.
- Apply PECS (**Producer Extends, Consumer Super**) whenever designing Java/Kotlin/C# collection APIs.
- Extract non-generic inner functions (`_impl(bytes: &[u8])`) in Rust/C++ libraries to prevent monomorphization bloat.
- Ban raw types and unchecked casts in Java CI (`-Xlint:unchecked -Werror`) to prevent delayed `ClassCastException`s.
- Use `cargo-bloat` (Rust) or `tsc --generateTrace` (TypeScript) if build times or binary sizes spike after adding generic abstractions.

interviewProblems.title: Type Systems & Generics
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Type Systems & Generics. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Generics parameterize types over other types so you write one algorithm or container while preserving static type safety, implemented via type erasure (Java), monomorphization (Rust/C++), or CLR reification (C#).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Erased Bytecode (Java / TS) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Monomorphized Bin (Rust / C+.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Monomorphized Bin (Rust / C+ experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Treat `-Xlint:unchecked` as a compiler error, ban raw types in lint rules, and use `Collections.checkedList` at untrusted boundaries.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Type erasure keeps binaries small but loses runtime type info and boxes primitives; monomorphization gives zero-cost specialization and inlining at the expense of compile time and binary size.
Avoid trap: Confusing `List<Object>` with `List<?>` in Java—`List<String>` is *not* a subtype of `List<Object>` because `List` is invariant.
Avoid trap: Trying to inspect `T.class` or instantiate `new T()` inside an erased Java generic method instead of passing a `Class<T>` token.
When to reach for it: Reusable containers, parsers, and algorithms (`Vec<T>`, `List<T>`, `Result<T, E>`) whose logic is independent of the element type.
When to reach for it: Encoding invariants at compile time via phantom types or bounded type parameters (e.g., `Connection<Authenticated>` vs `Connection<Unauthenticated>`).

putItTogether.title: Putting Type Systems Generics Together
putItTogether.summary: Type erasure keeps binaries small but loses runtime type info and boxes primitives; monomorphization gives zero-cost specialization and inlining at the expense of compile time and binary size.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Type Systems Generics before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Java's type erasure forces `Long` heap objects (16-byte object header + 8-byte payload + 4–8 byte reference = ~240–320 MB scattered on the heap with GC pressure); Rust's monomorphized `Vec<u64>` packs 80 MB contiguously in a single allocation with zero pointer chasing.
